sections.h2: Fairfield County offices for property tax
sections.html:
Three offices share the work here. The auditor sets values, the treasurer mails bills and takes payment, and the Board of Revision rules on value complaints. Nearly all of it happens in Lancaster, the county seat, in or near the building at 210 East Main Street.

Where to go for tax and recording questions

Both the treasurer and the auditor keep weekday counter hours of 8 to 4. The auditor assesses real property and administers levies and rates. Despite the title, the auditor has no legal authority to audit anyone, since that job belongs to the Auditor of State.

Southeast of Columbus, Fairfield County sits inside the Columbus metro area. Population was 158,921 in 2020 and is estimated at 169,752 for 2025, up 6.8%. Homes number 65,608, a typical owner-occupied one is valued at $298,800, and median household income is $90,966 (2020 to 2024).

Lancaster, Pickerington, Canal Winchester and Reynoldsburg are the main cities. Tax rates follow the taxing district, so similar houses can carry quite different bills. Buyers compare those bills, so pull yours before you pick a list price.

sections.h2: How the tax bill is calculated
sections.html:
The math runs in two steps. Take market value times 35% for assessed value, then multiply that by the effective rate for the parcel's taxing district to get gross tax. Which school district, township or city holds the parcel drives the rate.

Billing lags a year. A levy approved by voters counts for its own tax year, yet you pay it the year after. After a purchase, the old owner's name may appear on the next bill, since the record reflects whoever held the parcel on January 1. The new owner still has to pay it, so deal with proration at the closing table.

sections.h2: Due dates and how to pay
sections.html:
The tax comes due in two halves, one in February and one in July. For 2026 the dates were February 19 and July 30, and the treasurer posts each new year's schedule. A valid US Postal Service postmark on the due date keeps a mailed payment timely. Private postage meter marks and postdated checks are refused.

  • Mail a check made out to the Fairfield County Treasurer, using the return envelope sent with the bill.
  • Pay in person at 210 East Main Street, Room 105, or use the drive-thru and drop box at 135 W. Chestnut Street, which opens only for the three weeks before a due date.
  • Pay through MuniciPay online, where the e-check fee is $1.00 and cards cost 2.35%, or call the automated line at 740-279-3552.
  • Use the escrow plan to prepay in monthly installments. First-half escrow payments are based on the prior year's tax, and any difference is settled with the February payment.

Bills are mailed in January and June. Call 740-652-7140 if yours has not shown up by the end of January or mid June. A missing bill does not waive a penalty.

A late payment draws a 10% penalty on the current tax under ORC 323.17, reduced to 5% when it arrives within ten days of the due date. Interest is added to prior delinquencies on August 1 and to unpaid current tax on December 1.

Once a parcel is over a year delinquent, it can go to the county prosecutor for a sheriff's auction. Owners living in the house as their primary residence can ask for a delinquent tax contract to pay in installments, provided they have not defaulted on an earlier plan. The number for that is 740-652-7149. A penalty remission form exists too, but penalties can be forgiven only in limited circumstances set by law. The treasurer also publishes a delinquent parcel list and a notice about excess funds from tax foreclosure sales.

sections.h2: Disputing your value with the Board of Revision
sections.html:
Get the complaint form from the auditor's Board of Revision page, or call 740-652-7030 and ask for one. The filing window opens in December, once the first-half bill is mailed, and closes March 31. ORC 5715.19 sets the cutoff at March 31 or the close of first-half collection, whichever is later.

Once your form is in, the board mails a hearing date. Most owners go without a lawyer, and a hearing lasts under an hour. Bring a recent sale price, an appraisal or contractor repair estimates, because the board uses what you submit to revisit the appraised value.

sections.h2: Property records to pull before selling
sections.html:
Most of what a seller needs is online. The auditor's Real Estate Property Search shows each parcel's value and a Tax tab with the amount due, a Pay This Amount button and prior-year payments in parentheses. The treasurer's site carries the property tax search, the tax FAQ and the delinquent parcel list.

The recorder's land records search holds indexes back to 1800 and documents online from January 1980. Free property fraud and notary fraud alerts are available too, and they suit anyone holding a vacant or inherited house. Recorder staff will not run searches or help draft documents, and recording forms are not supplied, so paperwork goes through a title company or attorney. Call 740-652-7100.

  • Auditor: parcel number, current value, credits shown on the Tax tab.
  • Treasurer: balance due, escrow account, payment history for escrow customers by phone.
  • Recorder: deed copies, recorded mortgages and releases, fraud alert sign-up.

sections.h2: Tax credits that can affect a sale
sections.html:
The county has forms for three reductions: homestead for elderly or disabled owners, a farmland valuation for land being farmed, and the owner-occupancy credit. The auditor handles the applications at 740-652-7020. If someone online pushes a federal Senior Homeowner Tax Review Request, ignore it. The auditor has said no such federal form exists.

When a deed is filed, ORC 319.202 makes the buyer's value statement report whether the seller says the property carries a reduction and whether it was in agricultural use. If farm valuation applies, a recoupment charge may follow, so a seller with acreage should raise it with the closing agent before accepting a contract.

Owing tax does not block a sale, but the balance must be paid at closing. Your title company asks the treasurer for a payoff figure and deducts it from your proceeds before the deed is recorded. Look at the Tax tab on the auditor's search, then call 740-652-7140 for an exact number, because penalty and interest dates can move the total.

A cash buyer skips the lender's appraisal and most of the underwriting wait, which matters when a delinquency is heading toward a sheriff's sale. The tax balance still gets settled through the title company, so gather your latest bill and any payment plan papers first.

faqs.q: Where do I pay Fairfield County property taxes in person?
faqs.a: Visit the Treasurer's Office, Room 105 at 210 East Main Street in Lancaster, OH 43130, on a weekday from 8 to 4. The drive-thru at 135 W. Chestnut Street operates only in the three weeks before a due date.

faqs.q: When are Fairfield County property taxes due?
faqs.a: Half is due each February and the rest each July. In 2026 those were February 19 and July 30. The treasurer at 740-652-7140 can confirm the dates on your current bill.

faqs.q: What fee does Fairfield County charge to pay online?
faqs.a: MuniciPay charges $1.00 per e-check and 2.35% per card payment. A mailed check or a counter payment skips that fee.

faqs.q: Does the previous owner's name on my Fairfield County bill matter?
faqs.a: No, it does not shift the debt. The January 1 owner's name stays on the bill for a year, and the new owner still has to pay it.

faqs.q: Can I pay Fairfield County delinquent taxes in installments?
faqs.a: Yes, when the home is your primary residence and you have not defaulted on an earlier plan. Call 740-652-7149 or submit the Delinquent Payment Plan Request Form.
